records.title: Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and muscle hypertrophy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.abstract: We pooled 15 studies (n=390) comparing weekly set volumes for muscle hypertrophy. Each additional weekly set per muscle was associated with a 0.37% increase in muscle size. Performing 10 or more weekly sets per muscle produced larger gains than fewer than 5 weekly sets (effect size difference 0.24). Participants were mostly young untrained and recreationally trained men.
records.full_text: Methods: Randomized trials lasting at least 6 weeks that compared two or more weekly set volumes in healthy adults were included. Results: A graded dose-response was observed. Each additional weekly set per muscle was associated with a 0.37% increase in muscle size. Ten or more weekly sets per muscle produced larger gains than fewer than 5 weekly sets (ES difference 0.24, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.44). No study was industry funded.

records.title: Resistance training volume enhances muscle hypertrophy in trained men: a randomized trial of 6, 18 and 30 weekly sets
records.abstract: Thirty-four resistance-trained men were randomized to 6, 18 or 30 weekly sets per muscle for 8 weeks. Muscle thickness of the elbow flexors, triceps and quadriceps increased in a dose-dependent manner, with the 30-set group showing the largest gains. Strength gains were similar across groups.
records.full_text: Methods: 34 resistance-trained men (mean training age 4.4 years) were randomized to low (6 sets/week), moderate (18 sets/week) or high (30 sets/week) volume for 8 weeks. Results: Quadriceps muscle thickness increased by 6.8% in the high-volume group versus 2.1% in the low-volume group. 1RM squat and bench press gains did not differ between groups. Funding: none declared.

records.title: Twelve versus twenty-four weekly sets: hypertrophy plateaus at higher training volumes in trained adults
records.abstract: Forty trained adults (22 men, 18 women) performed either 12 or 24 weekly sets for the quadriceps for 12 weeks. Both groups increased vastus lateralis cross-sectional area, with no significant difference between 12 and 24 sets (5.1% vs 5.6%). The authors suggest that hypertrophy levels off around 12 to 20 weekly sets in trained individuals.
records.full_text: Methods: 40 trained adults (22 men, 18 women; at least 2 years of training) were randomized to 12 or 24 weekly sets for the quadriceps for 12 weeks. Results: Vastus lateralis cross-sectional area increased 5.1% with 12 sets and 5.6% with 24 sets (p=0.61). Perceived recovery scores were worse in the 24-set group.
records.journal: Fixture European Journal of Exercise Science

records.title: The resistance training volume dose-response for hypertrophy and strength: Bayesian meta-regressions (preprint)
records.abstract: Meta-regression of 67 studies found that hypertrophy keeps increasing with weekly set volume but with diminishing returns per additional set, while strength gains plateau at lower volumes of around 5 to 10 weekly sets. This preprint has not been peer reviewed.
records.full_text: Results: Across 67 studies (n=2058), hypertrophy increased with weekly sets with diminishing returns; the marginal gain per set fell by roughly half between 10 and 20 sets. Strength plateaued at approximately 5 to 10 weekly sets. This preprint has not been peer reviewed.

records.title: One versus three sets of resistance training for muscle hypertrophy in untrained young women
records.abstract: Twenty-eight untrained women performed 1 or 3 sets per exercise, twice per week, for 10 weeks. Three sets produced greater increases in muscle thickness than 1 set (4.9% vs 2.4%).
records.full_text: Methods: 28 untrained women aged 18-30 were randomized to 1 or 3 sets per exercise, twice weekly for 10 weeks. Results: Muscle thickness increased 4.9% with 3 sets and 2.4% with 1 set.

records.title: Extreme weekly set volumes of 50 sets maximize hypertrophy in trained men
records.abstract: Trained men performing 50 weekly sets gained twice as much muscle as those performing 20 sets. RETRACTED: this article was retracted due to data irregularities.

records.title: Progressive overload volume and muscle hypertrophy in a rat ladder-climbing model
records.abstract: Rats performing higher training volume on a weighted ladder-climbing protocol showed greater plantaris muscle hypertrophy than low-volume rats after 8 weeks.

records.title: Protein supplementation and resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.abstract: Meta-analysis of 49 randomized trials (n=1863). Protein supplementation augmented resistance training-induced gains in fat-free mass by 0.30 kg. Gains plateaued at a total protein intake of about 1.6 g/kg/day (95% CI 1.03 to 2.20).
records.full_text: Results: Protein supplementation increased fat-free mass gains by 0.30 kg (95% CI 0.09 to 0.52). Segmental regression identified a breakpoint at 1.62 g/kg/day of total protein intake, beyond which further protein produced no additional fat-free mass gain. Effects were smaller in older and untrained individuals.
records.journal: Fixture British Journal of Sports Nutrition

records.title: Higher protein intake during an energy deficit preserves lean mass: a randomized trial
records.abstract: Forty overweight young men in a 40% energy deficit with resistance training consumed 2.4 or 1.2 g/kg/day protein for 4 weeks. The higher-protein group gained 1.2 kg lean mass while the lower-protein group gained 0.1 kg; fat loss was greater with higher protein (4.8 vs 3.5 kg).
records.full_text: Methods: 40 young men (BMI 25-30) followed a 40% energy deficit with 6 days/week of resistance and interval training for 4 weeks, consuming 2.4 or 1.2 g/kg/day protein. Results: Lean body mass increased 1.2 kg with 2.4 g/kg and 0.1 kg with 1.2 g/kg. Fat mass decreased 4.8 kg and 3.5 kg respectively. Funding: supported by a dairy industry council.
records.journal: Fixture American Journal of Clinical Sports Nutrition

records.title: Training frequency does not affect hypertrophy when weekly volume is equated: a meta-analysis
records.abstract: Across 25 studies, training a muscle group once, twice or three or more times per week produced similar hypertrophy when weekly set volume was equated. Without volume equation, higher frequency was associated with larger gains, mediated by higher volume.
records.full_text: Results: With weekly volume equated, effect sizes did not differ by frequency (p=0.42). In non-equated studies, higher frequencies were associated with greater hypertrophy, explained by greater weekly sets.

records.title: Habitual protein intake and lean mass in older adults: a prospective cohort study
records.abstract: In 2066 adults aged 70-79 followed for 3 years, those in the highest quintile of protein intake (about 1.2 g/kg/day) lost 40% less lean mass than those in the lowest quintile (about 0.8 g/kg/day).
records.journal: Fixture Journal of Gerontology and Nutrition
